headline: FCC proposes new rule to end anonymous burner phones with mandatory KYC requirements
summary: The proposal would require cellular providers to collect name, address, government ID, and an alternate phone number from all customers, threatening a last bastion of digital anonymity.
details: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has proposed a new rule to implement "know-your-customer" (KYC) requirements for cellular networks. This aims to end the ability to obtain phone numbers without revealing identifying information.

Under the proposal, cellular providers would be required to obtain and retain the name, physical address, government-issued identification number, and an alternate telephone number. This data collection would apply to any new and renewing customer before granting access to services.

The FCC describes this measure as akin to money-laundering laws, designed to make it more difficult for scammers to exploit phone networks. It seeks to prevent illicit actors from using anonymous phone numbers for fraudulent activities.

Privacy advocates, however, argue that the rule threatens a last conduit of anonymity for various groups. This includes journalists, whistleblowers, activists, and individuals seeking to avoid mass data collection.

The new rule would directly impact services like Phreeli, a phone carrier allowing users to register with only a ZIP code. Phreeli's founder aims to help people avoid feeling watched and exploited by giant surveillance and data mining operations.
caption:
The FCC is proposing a new rule that could effectively end anonymous burner phones in the US. It would require cellular providers to collect extensive personal data from all customers.
